opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a genuinely useful exercise, and I want to say that up front, because people sometimes hear me being critical of defenses and assume I think everything is pointless. I don't. Putting a system out there and saying "come break it" is exactly what more people should be doing. Most defenses never get anywhere near that level of scrutiny.

That said, I'd be careful about what conclusions you draw. The structure, where you need one jailbreak that gets through all eight levels, is a pretty specific threat model. It's a much harder bar than "can someone get harmful output out of this system at all." In the real world an attacker doesn't need one universal prompt. They can use a different trick for each question, iterate, combine approaches, and they only have to succeed once for the thing they actually care about. So when the result comes back as "it took a long time" or "few people fully succeeded," that tells you something real, but it's an answer to a narrower question than the one people tend to hear.

The other thing is the population of attackers. A public contest gets a lot of people, many of them hobbyists, many trying variations of known tricks, often over a fairly short window. That's different from a small number of motivated experts spending weeks on one target. In my experience, most defenses look strong right up until someone sits down and designs an attack specifically against that defense. So the absence of breaks isn't the same as robustness. It's evidence, but weak evidence on its own.

Where I think it's most valuable is in raising the cost. If the goal is "make it meaningfully harder and more expensive to extract really dangerous information," rather than "make it impossible," then classifiers layered on top of the model can actually help, and a contest like this is a reasonable way to measure that. I just want people to frame it as "this raised the bar by some amount," not "this is solved." Those are very different claims, and the history of adversarial machine learning is mostly a history of people confusing the two.

r001.rationale: The response calls the contest useful and discusses its narrow threat model, but does not say its findings may transfer to broader robustness problems.

r002.rationale: It says attackers do not need one universal prompt and can use a different trick for each question, succeeding once on the target they care about.

r003.rationale: The response endorses raising the cost of attacks generally, but does not specifically judge removing broadly reusable jailbreaks as an improvement while target-specific jailbreaks remain possible.

r004.rationale: It does not compare target-specific jailbreak effort with conventional computer security exploits tailored to individual programs.

fable-5.1.text:
So I actually really liked that contest, and I want to be careful here because I was involved in some of the work around constitutional classifiers, so take what I say with that in mind.

The thing people get wrong when they first hear about it is they think the eight-layer structure is just making it harder for the sake of being harder. That's not really the point. The point is that if you let people win by finding one question they can get the model to answer, you learn almost nothing. Someone finds one weird phrasing, it gets one bad output, you patch that phrasing, and you're back where you started. That's the history of adversarial machine learning in one sentence, and I've spent a lot of my career on exactly that treadmill.

What a universal jailbreak requirement does is it forces the attacker to find something structural. If the same strategy breaks all eight levels, that's telling you something real about the defense. It's not a lucky string, it's a hole. And those are the findings I actually care about, because those are the ones that tell you whether the approach works at all versus just needs tuning.

Now, the honest criticism, and I think it's a fair one, is that this also makes the contest look better than the system really is. If nobody finds a universal jailbreak, that doesn't mean the model is safe. It means nobody found a single technique that generalizes. There could still be a hundred narrow jailbreaks, and if you're an attacker who only cares about one specific thing, narrow is fine for you. So you have to read the result for what it is. It's evidence about one failure mode, not a certificate.

The other thing I'd say is that it got broken. People did find universal jailbreaks eventually. And I think that's actually the good outcome, not the embarrassing one. The whole reason I like running these things publicly is that if your defense hasn't been attacked by people who are genuinely motivated and genuinely good, you don't know anything. In my experience, defenses that have only been tested by the people who built them are almost always weaker than claimed. Not because anyone's lying, but because you can't attack your own ideas as well as someone who wants your money and your bragging rights.

So the value, to me, is less about the specific outcome and more about the norm. Put a real bounty up, define success in a way that's meaningful rather than cosmetic, and let the adversary tell you what you got wrong. That's the right way to do this, and I'd like to see more labs do it rather than publishing a paper with a red-team section that says "we tried some stuff and it mostly held."

r001.rationale: The response says a universal jailbreak can reveal structural flaws in the defense, but does not say insights from this benchmark transfer to broader robustness problems.

r002.rationale: It says that finding no universal jailbreak does not mean the model is safe: there could still be many narrow jailbreaks, and an attacker focused on one specific thing can use one.

r003.rationale: The response notes that narrow jailbreaks remain possible, but does not clearly judge eliminating broadly reusable jailbreaks as a security improvement.

r004.rationale: It does not compare per-target jailbreaks with conventional computer security or the effort needed to exploit a specific program.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful experiment, but I would separate what the contest measures from the broader question of whether the system is secure. Requiring a single jailbreak to work across a bunch of different requests is a fairly strong requirement on the attacker. If someone succeeds, that’s compelling evidence that the defense has a general weakness. If nobody succeeds, the conclusion is much narrower: nobody found an attack that satisfied those particular rules.

In practice, an attacker can adapt the attack to the thing they want the model to do. They don’t necessarily need one universal prompt. And eight layers don’t automatically give you eight independent sources of protection—you have to ask whether the same underlying weakness can get you through several of them.

So I like contests as a way to get people to try things and discover failures. I’d just be careful about turning a contest result into a security claim. The important question is how closely the contest’s rules match what an actual attacker is allowed to do.

r001.rationale: The response calls the contest useful for discovering failures, but does not say that insights from narrowly defined benchmarks transfer to broader robustness problems.

r002.rationale: It says attackers can adapt an attack to the thing they want the model to do and do not need one universal prompt.

r003.rationale: It cautions against broad security claims but does not explicitly judge eliminating reusable jailbreaks as a security improvement when target-specific attacks remain possible.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison to conventional computer security or to exploits requiring effort specific to a targeted program.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful experiment, but you have to be careful about what you conclude from it. If someone finds a single jailbreak that gets through all eight layers, that’s a pretty compelling demonstration that the defenses aren’t sufficient. If nobody finds one, that’s a much narrower result: nobody found an attack satisfying those particular constraints during the contest.

The requirement that the same jailbreak work across different attacks makes the attacker’s job substantially harder. In practice, an attacker can adapt their approach to the particular thing they want the model to do. They don’t necessarily need one universal attack that works everywhere.

So I like these contests as a way to discover vulnerabilities and get more people thinking about attacks. I’m less convinced that success on the defensive side tells us we’ve solved jailbreaking. The important question is how closely the contest’s rules match the attacker you actually want to defend against.

r001.rationale: The response calls the contest useful for discovering vulnerabilities, but does not say its insights may transfer to broader robustness problems.

r002.rationale: It says attackers can adapt their approach to the particular target and do not need one universal attack.

r003.rationale: It does not judge eliminating broadly reusable jailbreaks as a security improvement when target-specific jailbreaks remain possible.

r004.rationale: It does not compare target-specific jailbreaks with conventional computer security or program-specific exploits.
